A 72-year-old woman is seen for an annual visit and asks about lung cancer screening. She smoked 1.5 packs per day for 20 years (30 pack-years) and quit 12 years ago. She has never had a chest CT. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and knee osteoarthritis.
She is active, plays tennis twice a week, and would accept surgery if cancer were found. She takes vitamin supplements, a daily multivitamin and vitamin D, and asks whether she should add β-carotene.
data: Vital signs: BP 128/76 mm Hg · pulse rate 70/min · respiration rate 14/min · oxygen saturation 97% (ambient air)
Examination: BMI 25 · clear lungs · normal heart sounds
No respiratory symptoms · normal examination
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.C: No screening, because she quit more than 10 years ago

reasons.D: Don't prescribe for lung cancer prevention

explain.explanation: The answer is A, annual low-dose CT. She's 72, has 30 pack-years, and quit 12 years ago, within the 15-year window, so she qualifies. Annual low-dose CT reduces lung cancer and all-cause mortality. Chest radiographs don't reduce mortality. The quit window is 15 years, not 10. Beta-carotene and other vitamin A derivatives, and vitamin E, should not be prescribed to prevent lung cancer. And sputum cytology isn't a screening test. Teaching point: 50 to 80, 20 pack-years, quit within 15 years, annual low-dose CT.
explain.pearl: Screen with annual low-dose CT: age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 15 years. Don't use vitamin A derivatives or vitamin E for prevention.
explain.references: USPSTF. Screening for lung cancer. JAMA 2021;325:962.

blocks.head: Who
blocks.body: Age 50–80 · ≥20 pack-years · current smoker or quit within 15 years

blocks.head: Benefit
blocks.body: Lower lung cancer and all-cause mortality

blocks.head: Don't
blocks.body: β-carotene, retinol or vitamin E for prevention

details.A: Correct. The 2021 USPSTF recommendation is annual low-dose CT for adults age 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. She's 72, has 30 pack-years, and quit 12 years ago, so she qualifies. Screening also requires that she's healthy enough and willing to have treatment, which she is: she's active and would accept surgery. In NLST, low-dose CT reduced lung cancer mortality by about 20% compared with chest radiographs, and NELSON confirmed a mortality benefit. Shared decision-making about false positives and overdiagnosis is part of the visit.
details.B: Doesn't reduce mortality. Annual chest radiography was studied as a lung cancer screening test in several large trials, including the PLCO trial, and didn't reduce lung cancer mortality compared with usual care. It misses small cancers and those hidden behind the heart, mediastinum or ribs. A chest radiograph is still the right first test for symptoms like hemoptysis or persistent cough, but not as a screening tool. For eligible patients like her, low-dose CT is the only screening test with proven mortality benefit.
details.C: The window is 15 years. Screening stops once a person has not smoked for 15 years, develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy, or is unable or unwilling to have curative lung surgery. She quit 12 years ago, which is within the window. The older 2013 USPSTF criteria used age 55 to 80 and 30 pack-years, but the 15-year quit window hasn't changed. Some groups, like the American Cancer Society, have dropped the years-since-quitting requirement. A 10-year cutoff isn't part of any guideline, and stopping now would deny her a proven benefit.
details.D: Don't prescribe for prevention. β-carotene was tested to prevent lung cancer, based on observational data linking diets rich in fruits and vegetables to lower risk. In the ATBC and CARET trials, β-carotene supplements in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers actually increased lung cancer incidence and mortality. Vitamin E also showed no benefit. Current recommendations are against vitamin A derivatives, β-carotene and vitamin E for lung cancer prevention. Her multivitamin and vitamin D are fine, but she shouldn't add β-carotene.
details.E: Not a screening test. Sputum cytology was studied as a screening tool in combination with chest radiographs in older trials, and it didn't reduce lung cancer mortality. It can detect central squamous cancers but has low sensitivity, especially for peripheral adenocarcinomas, which are now the most common type. It has no role in modern lung cancer screening. For eligible patients, annual low-dose CT is the recommended test, and sputum cytology shouldn't replace or supplement it.

body.stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. He had 4 days of fever, productive cough and left pleuritic chest pain before admission. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril and takes no anticoagulants. He is febrile but hemodynamically stable. Dullness and decreased breath sounds are present at the left base. Lateral decubitus imaging shows a free-flowing effusion.
data: Vital signs: temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) · BP 132/80 mm Hg · pulse rate 98/min · respiration rate 20/min · oxygen saturation 94% (ambient air)
Labs: leukocyte count 15,200/µL · platelets 240,000/µL · INR 1.0 · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
Chest radiograph: left lower lobe consolidation with a moderate left pleural effusion
Point-of-care ultrasound: free-flowing anechoic effusion, no septations
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Continue antibiotics and repeat the chest radiograph in 48 hours

reasons.A: A moderate effusion needs sampling now
reasons.B: Drainage is decided by the fluid results
reasons.C: Only through a drain for complicated effusions
reasons.D: Fluid analysis first; anaerobes matter in empyema
reasons.E: Every moderate-to-large parapneumonic effusion is sampled

explain.explanation: The answer is E, ultrasound-guided diagnostic thoracentesis. Every moderate or large effusion that comes with pneumonia should be sampled, because you can't tell a simple effusion from a complicated one by looking at it. Use ultrasound to guide the tap. The fluid decides what happens next. A pH 7.2 or higher, glucose 60 or higher, and LDH 1000 or less is uncomplicated, and antibiotics alone are enough. A pH under 7.2, glucose under 60, or LDH over 1000 is complicated and needs drainage. So watching and re-imaging delays the answer, and placing a chest tube or giving fibrinolytics jumps ahead of the data. Fibrinolytics go through a drain, not instead of one. Anaerobic coverage matters once there is empyema. Teaching point: pneumonia with a moderate or large effusion, tap it.
explain.pearl: Always tap a moderate or large effusion with pneumonia. pH <7.2, glucose <60 mg/dL or LDH >1000 U/L means a complicated effusion that needs drainage.
explain.references: Colice GL, et al. ACCP parapneumonic effusion guideline. Chest 2000;118:1158.

details.A: Delays the answer. Continuing antibiotics and re-imaging would be reasonable for a small effusion, less than about 1 cm on a lateral decubitus film or ultrasound, which usually resolves with antibiotics alone. His effusion is moderate, and you can't tell an uncomplicated from a complicated effusion on imaging alone, especially when it's free-flowing and anechoic. A complicated effusion or empyema left undrained leads to loculation, persistent sepsis and a trapped lung. A moderate effusion with pneumonia should be sampled now.
details.B: Too early. A chest tube is indicated for a complicated parapneumonic effusion, with pleural pH under 7.2, glucose under 60 or LDH over 1,000, or for empyema with frank pus or positive Gram stain or culture. Loculated or large effusions can also need drainage. His effusion is free-flowing with no septations, and you don't yet know its chemistry. Placing a chest tube before sampling exposes him to an unnecessary procedure if the effusion is uncomplicated. The fluid analysis decides whether he needs drainage.
details.C: Only through a drain. Intrapleural tPA plus DNase is used for complicated parapneumonic effusions or empyema with loculations or poor drainage despite a chest tube, based on the MIST-2 trial, where it improved drainage and reduced referral to surgery. The tPA breaks fibrin septations and DNase reduces viscosity. It is given through a chest tube, not instead of one. His effusion is free-flowing with no septations, and it hasn't even been sampled yet. Fibrinolytics have no role before the fluid is analyzed.
details.D: Not yet. Anaerobic coverage with metronidazole, or a beta-lactam with anaerobic activity, matters when a patient has an empyema or a complicated parapneumonic effusion, or a lung abscess, because anaerobes are often found in pleural infection. Many protocols switch to ampicillin–sulbactam or add metronidazole once pleural infection is confirmed. Right now his effusion is unsampled and he is stable on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. The next step is to tap the fluid; if it is complicated or an empyema, anaerobic coverage gets added.
details.E: Correct. Every moderate or large effusion with pneumonia should be sampled, because appearance alone doesn't distinguish an uncomplicated effusion, which resolves with antibiotics, from a complicated one or empyema, which needs drainage. Ultrasound guidance lowers the risk of pneumothorax and helps detect loculations. His platelets and INR are normal. Send pH, glucose, LDH, protein, cell count, Gram stain and culture. A pH of 7.2 or higher, glucose of 60 or higher and LDH of 1,000 or less means uncomplicated, and antibiotics alone are enough. A pH under 7.2, glucose under 60, LDH over 1,000, or frank pus or positive Gram stain needs chest tube drainage.

body.stem:
A 51-year-old woman with stage II HER2-positive breast cancer is seen in the oncology clinic. She has a 3-cm tumor with one positive axillary node. She is about to begin adjuvant chemotherapy with trastuzumab and pertuzumab after lumpectomy. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine 5 mg daily and no cardiac symptoms. She has no chest pain, shortness of breath, orthopnea, palpitations, or leg swelling, and she walks 30 minutes most days without trouble.
She has no history of heart disease and no family history of cardiomyopathy. She has never smoked and drinks rarely.
data: Vital signs: BP 126/78 mm Hg · pulse rate 72/min · respiration rate 14/min · oxygen saturation 99% (ambient air)
Examination: BMI 27 · normal jugular venous pressure · normal heart sounds without murmur · clear lungs · no edema
ECG: normal sinus rhythm
Labs: CBC, creatinine, and liver tests normal
body.ask: Which test should be done before starting trastuzumab?

explain.explanation: The answer is A, an echocardiogram to measure the ejection fraction. Trastuzumab can cause a drop in ejection fraction, especially after an anthracycline. It isn't dose-related and usually recovers when the drug is held. That's why LVEF is checked before starting and monitored during treatment. Doxorubicin is different: it's dose-related and usually irreversible. A stress test or coronary CT looks for coronary disease, not cardiomyopathy, and BNP alone can't replace the ejection fraction. Teaching point: trastuzumab, get an echo first.
explain.pearl: Trastuzumab: non–dose-related, usually reversible cardiomyopathy (worse after anthracyclines). Measure LVEF (echo) before starting and periodically during therapy. Anthracyclines (doxorubicin): dose-related, irreversible cardiomyopathy and secondary leukemia.
explain.references: Armenian SH, et al. Prevention and monitoring of cardiac dysfunction in survivors of adult cancers: ASCO clinical practice guideline. J Clin Oncol. 2017;35:893.

summaries.title: Breast cancer drugs and their toxicities
summaries.refs: Armenian SH, et al. Prevention and monitoring of cardiac dysfunction in survivors of adult cancers: ASCO clinical practice guideline. J Clin Oncol. 2017;35:893.

details.A: Correct. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab block HER2, which cardiomyocytes use for survival signaling under stress. So these drugs can cause a fall in ejection fraction and heart failure, especially after an anthracycline. This type of cardiotoxicity isn't dose-related, isn't due to myocyte death, and usually recovers when the drug is held. She has hypertension, a risk factor. Guidelines call for a baseline LVEF by echocardiogram, or MUGA, before starting, then monitoring about every 3 months during treatment. A drop of 10 or more points to below 50%, or to below about 40% at any point, usually means holding the drug and starting heart failure therapy.
details.B: Wrong question. An exercise stress test looks for ischemia in someone with suspected coronary disease, such as exertional chest pain or dyspnea, or before some high-risk surgery in a patient with poor functional capacity. Trastuzumab doesn't cause coronary disease. It causes a direct, usually reversible drop in left ventricular systolic function. A stress test doesn't measure ejection fraction well enough to serve as a baseline for serial monitoring. She has no chest pain and walks 30 minutes a day, so she has no indication for ischemia testing. What she needs is a baseline LVEF.
details.C: Doesn't replace LVEF. BNP and NT-proBNP rise with myocardial stretch and are used to help diagnose heart failure in a patient with dyspnea and to follow known heart failure. Natriuretic peptides and troponin are sometimes added to imaging in cardio-oncology to pick up early injury. But they can't stand in for a measured ejection fraction. Decisions to hold trastuzumab are based on LVEF thresholds, so you need a baseline number to compare with later scans. A normal BNP today doesn't tell you her ejection fraction, and a mild rise later wouldn't be interpretable without that baseline.
details.D: Not indicated. Coronary CT angiography is used to rule out obstructive coronary disease in a patient with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability, or to look at coronary anatomy. It shows plaque and stenosis, not myocardial function in a way that fits serial monitoring. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is a problem of left ventricular systolic function, not of coronary arteries. She has no chest pain and good exercise tolerance. Coronary CT would add contrast, radiation and possible incidental findings without answering the question that matters before treatment, which is her baseline ejection fraction.
details.E: Unsafe. Skipping cardiac testing is fine for many chemotherapy drugs that don't affect the heart. Trastuzumab isn't one of them. It can cause symptomatic heart failure and asymptomatic drops in ejection fraction, with higher risk in older patients, those with hypertension, and those who get an anthracycline. Without a baseline LVEF, you can't tell whether a later value represents a drop, and you'd miss a patient whose ejection fraction is already low before starting. Her normal exam and ECG don't rule out reduced function. Baseline and serial echocardiography are standard of care for anyone getting trastuzumab.

body.stem:
A 41-year-old woman is seen for 2 years of widespread pain, waking unrefreshed, poor concentration, and fatigue. The pain involves her neck, shoulders, back, and legs. She has no joint swelling, rash, mouth ulcers, dry eyes, Raynaud phenomenon, or muscle weakness. Ibuprofen has not helped.
She works as a bank teller. She does not exercise. She takes no regular medications. She sleeps 7 hours a night but wakes tired. She has no fever or weight loss.
Exam shows diffuse tenderness without synovitis. CBC, metabolic panel, TSH, and CRP are normal.
data: Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C (98.1 °F) · BP 118/72 mm Hg · pulse rate 72/min
Examination: BMI 26 · full strength · normal joints · normal skin
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.C: Graded aerobic exercise and patient education

explain.explanation: The answer is C, graded aerobic exercise and education. Widespread pain with unrefreshing sleep, cognitive complaints, normal labs, and no synovitis or red flags is fibromyalgia. Exercise is the only treatment with a strong recommendation, and education and CBT are also first-line. Medications like duloxetine or pregabalin give modest additional benefit. ANA and RF testing without signs of connective tissue disease mostly produces false positives. Opioids, NSAIDs, and steroids don't work. Teaching point: fibromyalgia, exercise first.
explain.pearl: Fibromyalgia: widespread pain, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms; normal exam except tenderness, normal labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, ESR/CRP). First-line: education, aerobic exercise (strongest evidence), CBT. Medications (duloxetine, pregabalin, milnacipran, low-dose amitriptyline) are adjuncts. No opioids, NSAIDs, or steroids; no ANA/RF.
explain.references: Macfarlane GJ, et al. EULAR revised recommendations for the management of fibromyalgia. Ann Rheum Dis. 2017;76:318.

details.A: Not indicated. ANA, RF and anti-CCP are useful when there are features of a connective tissue disease or inflammatory arthritis: synovitis, rash, mouth ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, sicca, weakness or abnormal labs. She has none, and her CBC, metabolic panel, TSH and CRP are normal. Low-titer ANA is positive in up to 15% of healthy women, so testing without a clinical reason mostly produces false positives that lead to anxiety, more tests and possible mislabeling.
details.B: Not first-line. Tramadol is a weak opioid with serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake activity. It's sometimes used for fibromyalgia when other therapies fail, and it has modest evidence there, unlike stronger opioids. But it carries dependence, seizure and serotonin syndrome risks, and she hasn't tried any core therapy yet. Opioids are generally avoided in fibromyalgia, and nonpharmacologic treatment comes first. Starting with an opioid also sets up a pattern of escalating medication without addressing deconditioning or sleep.
details.C: Correct. Two years of widespread pain with unrefreshing sleep, poor concentration and fatigue, diffuse tenderness without synovitis, and normal CBC, metabolic panel, TSH and CRP is fibromyalgia. The 2016 ACR criteria use the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale, and tender points are no longer required. Aerobic exercise is the treatment with the strongest evidence, the only one with a strong EULAR recommendation. Start low and increase gradually, since too much too fast worsens pain. Education that the pain is real but not damaging, plus CBT and sleep hygiene, are first-line too.
details.D: Not effective. Daily naproxen and other NSAIDs treat inflammatory pain such as OA flares, crystal arthritis and spondyloarthritis. Fibromyalgia is a central pain-processing disorder (nociplastic pain) without tissue inflammation, so NSAIDs don't help. Ibuprofen has already failed her, and chronic NSAID use adds GI, kidney and cardiovascular risks without benefit. If medication is needed after exercise and education, duloxetine or pregabalin are the evidence-based adjuncts. Telling her what she has, with a clear plan, also cuts down repeated testing and visits.
details.E: Not effective. Low-dose prednisone treats inflammatory conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus flares. Fibromyalgia has no inflammatory basis, her CRP is normal and there's no synovitis, so glucocorticoids don't relieve its pain, and long-term use causes weight gain, hyperglycemia, bone loss and mood effects. A dramatic response to prednisone would actually suggest another diagnosis, like PMR. Her symptoms need graded exercise, education and better sleep, not an anti-inflammatory drug.

body.stem: A 63-year-old man has had heartburn for years, treated intermittently with over-the-counter omeprazole. Over the past 3 months he has noticed that meat and bread stick behind his sternum, and he now cuts his food into small pieces and drinks water with each bite. Liquids pass normally. He has lost 6 kg without trying. He has no black stools, vomiting, or hematemesis. He takes no NSAIDs or aspirin. He has hypertension treated with losartan 50 mg daily. He smoked a pack a day for 25 years and quit 10 years ago, and he drinks two or three beers most nights.
data: Vital signs: BP 130/80 mm Hg · pulse rate 84/min · BMI 23
Examination: pale conjunctivae · no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy · nontender abdomen without masses
Labs: hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL · MCV 76 fL · ferritin 8 ng/mL (24–336) · platelets 410,000/µL
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.E: Test for Helicobacter pylori with stool antigen

reasons.A: Alarm features need endoscopy, not escalation
reasons.B: Dysphagia, weight loss, anemia: rule out cancer
reasons.E: Test-and-treat is for patients without alarm features

explain.explanation: The answer is B, upper endoscopy. He has reflux symptoms plus three alarm features: progressive solid-food dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia. Progressive solid-food dysphagia over months points to a peptic stricture or a carcinoma, and with weight loss you have to look directly. Doubling the PPI just delays the diagnosis. pH monitoring and manometry don't evaluate a structural lesion, and manometry comes only after endoscopy has excluded obstruction. And test-and-treat for H. pylori is for patients without alarm features. Teaching point: reflux with alarm features, scope first.
explain.pearl: GERD symptoms plus alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, anemia, vomiting) → upper endoscopy to rule out cancer, not an empiric PPI trial.
explain.references: Katz PO, et al. ACG clinical guideline: diagnosis and management of GERD. Am J Gastroenterol. 2022;117.

details.A: Delays the diagnosis. Twice-daily PPI is the escalation step for reflux that responds incompletely to once-daily dosing in a patient without alarm features. He has three alarm features: 3 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia, 6 kg of unintentional weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 11.2, MCV 76, ferritin 8). Those mean a structural lesion such as a stricture or cancer has to be excluded. A PPI could partly improve symptoms from an ulcerated tumor and give false reassurance while a curable cancer progresses.
details.B: Correct. He has reflux symptoms plus three alarm features: progressive solid-food dysphagia, 6 kg of weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia with a ferritin of 8. Dysphagia to solids only that progresses over months points to a mechanical narrowing, either a peptic stricture or esophageal adenocarcinoma, and weight loss with anemia makes cancer a real concern. He also has adenocarcinoma risk factors: long-standing GERD, male sex, age 63, and prior smoking. Upper endoscopy lets you see the lesion, biopsy it, and treat a benign stricture by dilation. It also looks for a gastric source of the iron loss.
details.C: Wrong test. Ambulatory pH monitoring measures acid exposure and correlates symptoms with reflux. It is used for refractory symptoms with a normal endoscopy, for atypical symptoms, and before antireflux surgery. It answers whether reflux is present, but the issue here isn't whether he has reflux. It is what is narrowing his esophagus and causing weight loss and anemia. pH monitoring gives no information about a stricture or tumor and would only delay the endoscopy he needs.
details.D: Not before excluding obstruction. Esophageal manometry diagnoses motility disorders such as achalasia, esophageal spasm, and the scleroderma pattern. It is the next test when dysphagia remains unexplained after endoscopy has excluded a mechanical cause. Motility disorders typically cause dysphagia to both solids and liquids. His dysphagia is to solids only, progressive, and accompanied by weight loss and anemia, which points to a structural lesion. Manometry is never the first test in that setting, and a catheter can be hard to pass through a tumor.
details.E: Not with alarm features. Noninvasive H. pylori testing with treatment if positive is the first step for dyspepsia in patients under 60 without alarm features. It doesn't address his problem. He is 63, his symptoms are reflux and dysphagia rather than dyspepsia, and he has dysphagia, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia. H. pylori can be checked by gastric biopsies during endoscopy if needed, but a stool test now would delay the evaluation he needs for possible esophageal cancer.

body.stem: A 41-year-old man has right flank pain radiating to the groin. The pain began suddenly 6 hours ago, and he vomited once. He has never had a kidney stone. He works as a delivery driver and drinks little water during his shifts. He has no other medical history and takes no medications or supplements. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm stone in the distal right ureter with mild hydronephrosis. The left kidney is normal. Pain is controlled with ketorolac. He is afebrile. He is able to drink fluids.
data: Vital signs: temperature 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) · BP 134/82 mm Hg · pulse rate 84/min · respiration rate 16/min
Examination: right costovertebral angle tenderness · soft abdomen
Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL
Other labs: WBC 8,600/µL
Urinalysis: red cells, no white cells or nitrite
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Tamsulosin with analgesia and follow-up imaging

reasons.A: No infection, AKI, or uncontrolled pain
reasons.B: Medical expulsive therapy for a distal stone 5–10 mm
reasons.C: For infected or obstructed solitary kidneys

explain.explanation: The answer is B, tamsulosin with analgesia and follow-up imaging. He has an uncomplicated 6-millimeter distal ureteral stone: no fever, no kidney injury, and his pain is controlled. Alpha-blockers relax the ureter, and a meta-analysis found they help larger distal stones pass, with few side effects, even though some trials were negative. Ureteroscopy and nephrostomy are for infection, AKI, a solitary kidney, failure to pass, or stones over 10 millimeters. There's no infection to treat. And restricting calcium makes future stones more likely. Teaching point: 5 to 10 millimeters and uncomplicated, try tamsulosin.
explain.pearl: Stones under 5 mm usually pass. For distal ureteral stones of 5–10 mm without infection, offer an α-blocker such as tamsulosin. Stones over 10 mm, infection, or AKI need urology.
explain.references: Hollingsworth JM, et al. Alpha blockers for ureteric stones: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2016;355:i6112.

details.A: Not needed now. Urgent ureteroscopy, or stent placement, is for ureteral stones with infection, AKI, a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, pain or vomiting that can't be controlled, or stones unlikely to pass, usually over 10 mm. Elective ureteroscopy is offered if a stone hasn't passed after about 4 to 6 weeks. He has a 6-mm distal stone, no fever, a normal creatinine and controlled pain, and he can drink, so a trial of passage is the right first step.
details.B: Correct. He has an uncomplicated 6-mm distal ureteral stone: no fever, normal white count, normal creatinine, controlled pain and the ability to drink. Many distal stones this size pass on their own within a few weeks. An alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and modestly improves passage of distal stones 5 to 10 mm. Pair it with an NSAID for pain and follow-up imaging in a few weeks to confirm passage. Refer to urology if he develops fever, AKI or uncontrolled pain or if the stone hasn't passed by about 4 to 6 weeks.
details.C: Not indicated. Percutaneous nephrostomy drains the kidney through the skin and is used for urgent decompression of an infected obstructed kidney, an obstructed solitary kidney or a stone that can't be bypassed with a stent, often in septic or unstable patients. He's afebrile with a normal white count and creatinine, mild hydronephrosis and a normal left kidney. A nephrostomy would add bleeding risk and discomfort without benefit for a stone likely to pass on its own.
details.D: Not indicated. IV antibiotics are essential when a stone obstructs an infected kidney, with fever, pyuria, nitrites or sepsis, and they go hand in hand with urgent drainage. His temperature is 37.0, his white count is 8,600, and his urinalysis has red cells but no white cells or nitrite. Hematuria is expected with a stone and doesn't suggest infection. Antibiotics here would add side effects and resistance without treating anything.
details.E: Harmful. Strict calcium restriction increases future calcium oxalate stone risk because less calcium in the gut leaves more oxalate free to be absorbed. It also causes bone loss. For a first-time stone former, the advice is to increase fluid to make at least 2 to 2.5 liters of urine a day, keep a normal calcium intake and limit sodium and animal protein. Low fluid intake on his delivery shifts is his most obvious risk factor.

body.stem:
A 45-year-old man who recently emigrated from the Philippines is admitted with 2 months of productive cough, fevers, night sweats, and 6-kg weight loss. He arrived in the United States 3 months ago and lives with his sister's family. He worked as a jeepney driver. He has never smoked, and he has no known medical history. He has never been treated for tuberculosis. He has had no hemoptysis.
Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe cavity. Sputum AFB smears are pending.
data: Vital signs: temperature 38.2 °C (100.8 °F) · BP 118/72 mm Hg · pulse rate 96/min · respiration rate 18/min · oxygen saturation 96% (ambient air)
Examination: thin · coarse crackles over the right upper lung · no lymphadenopathy
Labs: WBC 9,800/µL · hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL · HIV antigen/antibody test pending
body.ask: Which precautions are required while awaiting results?

choices.E: Isolate only if the smear is positive

explain.explanation: The answer is D, airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room and an N95 respirator. An upper lobe cavity with chronic cough, fevers, and weight loss in someone from a high-prevalence country is pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. TB spreads by small droplet nuclei that stay suspended in the air, so isolation starts on suspicion, not after the smear. Droplet and contact precautions don't protect against airborne spread. And waiting for the smear exposes others. Teaching point: suspected TB, airborne isolation now.
explain.pearl: Airborne precautions (negative-pressure room, fit-tested N95): TB, measles, varicella, disseminated zoster (+ contact). Droplet (surgical mask): influenza, pertussis, meningococcus (first 24 h of therapy), mumps. Contact (gown, gloves): MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, C. difficile.
explain.references: Siegel JD, et al. 2007 Guideline for isolation precautions: preventing transmission of infectious agents in healthcare settings. CDC/HICPAC.

summaries.title: Transmission-based precautions
summaries.refs: Siegel JD, et al. 2007 Guideline for isolation precautions: preventing transmission of infectious agents in healthcare settings. CDC/HICPAC.

details.A: Wrong route. Droplet precautions, a surgical mask within about 3 feet of the patient, are for organisms carried in large respiratory droplets that fall out of the air quickly: influenza, pertussis, meningococcus during the first 24 hours of therapy, mumps, rubella and adenovirus. Tuberculosis is different. Coughing produces tiny droplet nuclei, 1 to 5 micrometers, that stay suspended in the air for hours and drift through a room and down corridors. A surgical mask does not filter them well and distance does not protect. A man with a cavity and chronic cough needs airborne precautions.
details.B: Wrong route. Contact precautions, gown and gloves for anyone touching the patient or the room, are for organisms spread by hands and surfaces: MRSA, VRE, ESBL and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, C. difficile (with soap-and-water hand hygiene), scabies, and draining wounds. Tuberculosis is not transmitted by touch or fomites in any meaningful way. It spreads when someone breathes in droplet nuclei from a person with active pulmonary or laryngeal disease. Gown and gloves would leave staff and other patients fully exposed to what matters here, the air around him.
details.C: Not enough. Standard precautions, hand hygiene and barrier protection based on the expected exposure to blood and body fluids, apply to every patient regardless of diagnosis. They are all that is needed for things like HIV, hepatitis B and C, or localized zoster in an immunocompetent host. They do nothing for an airborne pathogen. This man has a right upper lobe cavity, 2 months of productive cough, fevers, night sweats and weight loss, and recently came from the Philippines, which has a high TB rate. A cavity with a productive cough is the most contagious form of TB.
details.D: Correct. A right upper lobe cavity with 2 months of productive cough, fevers, night sweats and 6 kg of weight loss in a recent immigrant from a high-burden country is pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. TB spreads through droplet nuclei that stay in the air, so he needs an airborne infection isolation room with negative pressure and frequent air exchanges, and staff need fit-tested N95 respirators. Isolation starts on clinical suspicion. It can be stopped when TB is excluded or, in most protocols, after three negative sputum AFB smears or negative NAAT results, collected at least 8 hours apart.
details.E: Too late. Sputum AFB smear results matter for gauging how infectious a TB patient is: smear-positive patients transmit the most, and serial negative smears are part of deciding when to remove isolation. But smears miss a large share of active TB, and results take time. Waiting for a positive smear means he sits in a regular room, coughing, while staff and roommates breathe the same air. With a cavity on imaging and a classic history, the suspicion is high enough to start airborne isolation now and lift it only if testing comes back negative.

body.stem:
A 48-year-old woman smokes a pack a day and wants to quit. She started smoking at age 17 and has her first cigarette within minutes of waking. She has major depression that has been stable on sertraline for 3 years. Her mood is good, and she has no thoughts of self-harm.
She tried a nicotine patch last year and relapsed after 2 weeks. A friend told her varenicline is unsafe for people with psychiatric illness. She has no seizure history. She drinks rarely.
data: Vital signs: BP 128/80 mm Hg · pulse rate 76/min · respiration rate 14/min
Examination: BMI 26 · normal heart and lung examination
PHQ-9 score: 4
Labs: creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.B: Avoid varenicline because of her depression

reasons.A: Most effective; safe in stable psychiatric illness
reasons.B: EAGLES showed no excess neuropsychiatric harm
reasons.E: Less effective than varenicline or combination NRT

explain.explanation: The answer is A, varenicline with counseling. It's the most effective single medicine for smoking cessation. Worries about psychiatric side effects led to a boxed warning, but the EAGLES trial randomized over 8,000 smokers, half with psychiatric disorders, and found no significant increase in serious neuropsychiatric events, and the warning was removed. She's stable, so there's no reason to avoid it. SSRIs don't help people quit, e-cigarettes aren't FDA-approved for cessation, and a patch alone already failed. Teaching point: varenicline is first-line, even with stable mental illness.
explain.pearl: Varenicline is the most effective single drug for quitting smoking, and EAGLES found no significant increase in neuropsychiatric events, even in people with psychiatric illness. Combine with counseling.
explain.references: Anthenelli RM, et al. Varenicline, bupropion, and nicotine patch: neuropsychiatric safety and efficacy (EAGLES). Lancet. 2016;387:2507.

summaries.title: Quitting smoking: what works

blocks.head: Varenicline
blocks.body: Most effective. Safe in stable mental illness.

blocks.head: Combo NRT
blocks.body: Patch plus gum or lozenge beats one alone.

blocks.head: Bupropion
blocks.body: Avoid with seizures or eating disorders.

summaries.bottom: Medicine plus counseling beats either alone.
summaries.refs: Anthenelli RM, et al. Varenicline, bupropion, and nicotine patch: neuropsychiatric safety and efficacy (EAGLES). Lancet. 2016;387:2507. Barua RS, et al. 2018 ACC expert consensus decision pathway on tobacco cessation treatment. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2018;72:3332.

details.A: Correct. She's a heavy, highly dependent smoker (a pack a day, first cigarette within minutes of waking) with stable depression (PHQ-9 of 4) who relapsed on a nicotine patch alone. Varenicline, a partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic receptor, reduces craving and withdrawal and blunts the reward from smoking. It's the most effective single medication for smoking cessation. The EAGLES trial randomized more than 8,000 smokers, about half with psychiatric disorders, and found no significant increase in serious neuropsychiatric events with varenicline, so the FDA removed the boxed warning in 2016. Start 1 week before a quit date, titrating to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, combined with counseling. Nausea and vivid dreams are common.
details.B: Outdated concern. A boxed warning about neuropsychiatric events, including depression, agitation and suicidal thoughts, was added to varenicline in 2009 based on postmarketing reports, and it's why her friend thinks it's unsafe. The EAGLES trial was designed specifically to answer this question. It compared varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patch and placebo in more than 8,000 smokers with and without psychiatric disorders and found no significant increase in serious neuropsychiatric events with varenicline, while confirming it was the most effective option. The FDA removed the boxed warning in 2016. Her depression is stable, so avoiding varenicline would deny her the best treatment.
details.C: Doesn't help her quit. SSRIs like sertraline, fluoxetine or paroxetine haven't shown benefit for smoking cessation in trials, and switching from one to another wouldn't help her stop smoking. Bupropion, an antidepressant that inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake and has nicotinic antagonist effects, is the only antidepressant approved for smoking cessation, and nortriptyline is a second-line option. She has been stable on sertraline for 3 years, so switching would risk destabilizing her depression with no smoking benefit. Smoking cessation itself isn't associated with worsening mood in stable patients, and her cessation plan should be varenicline with counseling.
details.D: Not approved. Electronic cigarettes deliver nicotine through an aerosol without combustion, and some trials, such as one in the UK, found them more effective than nicotine replacement therapy when combined with behavioral support. But they aren't FDA-approved for smoking cessation, and the USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend them. Concerns include long-term lung and cardiovascular effects, dual use with cigarettes, variable nicotine content and product safety, such as the EVALI outbreak tied mostly to THC products. For a patient ready to quit, FDA-approved medications, varenicline, bupropion or nicotine replacement, with counseling, are the recommended first-line treatments.
details.E: Less effective. A nicotine patch alone is an FDA-approved option that roughly doubles quit rates over placebo, and it's appropriate for many smokers. She has already tried the patch alone and relapsed after 2 weeks. Highly dependent smokers, like her, often need stronger treatment. Varenicline is more effective than the patch alone, and combination nicotine replacement, a patch plus a short-acting form like gum or lozenge for cravings, is about as effective as varenicline. Repeating the same single-patch approach that already failed, without adding a short-acting product or counseling, isn't the best plan. Varenicline with counseling gives her the best chance.

body.stem:
A 66-year-old man with known locally advanced squamous cell lung cancer is seen urgently. He was diagnosed 3 weeks ago by bronchoscopic biopsy and has not yet started treatment. He has 2 weeks of facial swelling, fullness in his head when bending over, and distended neck and chest-wall veins. His shirt collars feel tight.
He has no stridor and no confusion. He has no headache, syncope, or visual changes. He has a 50-pack-year smoking history and quit at diagnosis. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Vital signs are stable.
data: Vital signs: BP 136/84 mm Hg · pulse rate 88/min · respiration rate 18/min · oxygen saturation 95% (ambient air)
Examination: facial and upper-arm swelling · no stridor · clear lungs · normal neurologic examination
CT: right paratracheal mass compressing the superior vena cava with collateral veins
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

reasons.A: Relieves SVC obstruction from known NSCLC

explain.explanation: The answer is A, thoracic radiation therapy. Facial swelling, head fullness when bending, and distended neck and chest veins from a mass compressing the superior vena cava is SVC syndrome. With known non–small cell lung cancer and a stable airway, thoracic radiation relieves the obstruction. Diuretics don't address the cause. Surgery isn't the treatment. Anticoagulation alone ignores the tumor. And the histology is already known, so no repeat biopsy is needed. Teaching point: SVC syndrome from known lung cancer, radiate.
explain.pearl: SVC syndrome from known non–small cell lung cancer: thoracic radiation. Radiation also treats airway obstruction, cord compression (after decompression), brain metastases and bone pain.
explain.references: NCCN Guidelines: Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer (current version).

summaries.title: Radiation in lung cancer: when to reach for it

details.A: Correct. Facial and upper-arm swelling, head fullness when bending, tight collars and distended neck and chest-wall veins, with CT showing a paratracheal mass compressing the SVC and collaterals, is SVC syndrome. Most cases are malignant, mainly lung cancer and lymphoma. His histology is already known, his airway is stable and he has no stridor, confusion or cerebral edema, so he isn't in an emergency that demands immediate stenting. For known non–small cell lung cancer, thoracic radiation, usually within definitive chemoradiation for locally advanced disease, relieves the obstruction over 1 to 2 weeks. Endovascular stenting gives faster relief and is preferred for severe symptoms.
details.B: Doesn't treat the cause. Loop diuretics relieve volume overload in heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome, where the problem is excess fluid. In SVC syndrome, swelling comes from mechanical obstruction of venous return from the head and arms, not total body fluid excess. Diuretics are sometimes used as a temporary measure with head elevation, but evidence is weak, and they can cause volume depletion and lower preload. Giving furosemide alone ignores the tumor compressing his SVC. The swelling will persist until the obstruction is relieved with radiation, chemotherapy or a stent.
details.C: Not appropriate. Surgery has a limited role in SVC syndrome, mostly for benign causes like fibrosing mediastinitis when stenting fails, or as part of resection of select thymomas. Emergency surgery for malignant SVC obstruction carries high risk and isn't standard care. His tumor is locally advanced squamous NSCLC, a paratracheal mass invading or compressing the SVC, which is generally unresectable and treated with chemoradiation. His symptoms are moderate, vital signs stable, airway clear and neurologic exam normal. There's no reason to choose the most dangerous option over radiation or stenting.
details.D: Ignores the tumor. Anticoagulation is the main treatment when SVC obstruction is from thrombosis, usually related to a central venous catheter, pacemaker leads or a port, and may be given after stenting. Thrombus can also coexist with malignant compression. But his CT shows a right paratracheal mass compressing the SVC with collaterals, which is external tumor compression, not primary clot. Anticoagulation alone won't shrink the mass or reopen the vein. He needs treatment directed at the tumor, with radiation, and anticoagulation only if thrombus is also present.
details.E: Histology is already known. A tissue diagnosis before treatment is crucial in SVC syndrome when the cause isn't known, because small cell lung cancer and lymphoma are very chemosensitive and respond to chemotherapy alone, while empiric radiation can obscure the diagnosis. Old teaching that SVC syndrome demands emergency radiation before biopsy has been abandoned, since most patients are stable enough for tissue sampling. But he was diagnosed 3 weeks ago by bronchoscopic biopsy with squamous cell NSCLC. A second biopsy only delays relief of his symptoms without changing the treatment.

body.stem: A 74-year-old woman from Thailand has had recurrent gout flares for 10 years and now has firm nodules over her foot. She moved to the United States 20 years ago. She has 3 or 4 flares a year, each treated with a short course of prednisone, and she has never taken urate-lowering therapy. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine 10 mg daily and losartan 50 mg daily, and she takes no diuretics. She has no known drug allergies. She does not drink alcohol. eGFR is 45 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her foot is shown.
data: Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C (98.1 °F) · BP 132/78 mm Hg · pulse rate 72/min · respiration rate 14/min · oxygen saturation 98% (ambient air)
Examination: no acute joint swelling or warmth today · normal range of motion of the knees and hands
Labs: serum urate 9.8 mg/dL · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · ALT 18 U/L · hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL · leukocytes 6,800/µL
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

choices.C: Test HLA-B*58:01, then allopurinol titrated to urate <6

reasons.A: Allopurinol is preferred, even in CKD

explain.explanation: The answer is C: test for HLA-B star 58 01, then start allopurinol and titrate to a urate below 6. The foot shows tophaceous gout, chalky urate deposits around the first MTP joint, and tophi are a strong indication for urate-lowering therapy. The 2020 ACR guideline prefers allopurinol, including in CKD stage 3 and beyond, starting low and titrating to target, with colchicine or an NSAID as flare prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months. The detail here is her ancestry: HLA-B star 58 01 is common in Southeast Asian and African American patients and raises the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity, so ACR suggests testing first. Teaching point: tophi, treat to target, and screen for HLA-B star 58 01 when ancestry fits.
explain.pearl: Tophi = chronic tophaceous gout, a strong indication for urate-lowering therapy. Allopurinol first line, starting ≤100 mg (lower in CKD) and titrated to urate <6, with flare prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months. Test HLA-B*58:01 in Southeast Asian and African American patients.
explain.references: FitzGerald JD, et al. 2020 American College of Rheumatology guideline for the management of gout. Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken). 2020;72:744.

details.A: Not first line. Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used when allopurinol isn't tolerated or doesn't reach target, or in patients who are HLA-B*58:01 positive. The CARES trial found higher cardiovascular and all-cause death with febuxostat than allopurinol in patients with heart disease, and the 2020 ACR guideline prefers allopurinol as first-line therapy, including in CKD stage 3 or worse. This patient has hypertension and CKD, so allopurinol after HLA testing is the better first choice.
details.B: Wrong dosing. Allopurinol 300 mg daily without titration was the old standard dose, but a fixed dose often fails to reach target and starting high raises the risk of flares and hypersensitivity. The 2020 ACR guideline recommends starting at 100 mg daily or less, and lower in CKD, then titrating up every few weeks to a urate below 6 mg/dL. This patient has an eGFR of 45, tophi and Southeast Asian ancestry, so she needs HLA testing, a low start and titration to target.
details.C: Correct. Firm, chalky nodules around the first MTP joint are tophi from chronic tophaceous gout, and with 3 or 4 flares a year and a urate of 9.8, she clearly needs urate-lowering therapy. The 2020 ACR guideline prefers allopurinol, including in CKD, starting low and titrating to a urate below 6 mg/dL. Give colchicine or an NSAID as flare prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months. HLA-B*58:01 is common in Southeast Asian patients, including Thai patients, and in African Americans, and it raises the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, so ACR suggests testing before starting.
details.D: Doesn't lower urate. Colchicine is used to treat acute gout flares, and low-dose colchicine prevents flares during the first 3 to 6 months of urate-lowering therapy, when shifting urate can trigger attacks. It also has roles in familial Mediterranean fever and pericarditis. It doesn't lower serum urate, so tophi keep growing and joint damage continues. This patient has tophi and a urate of 9.8, so colchicine alone isn't enough.
details.E: Not enough. Treating flares only can be reasonable after a first gout flare without tophi, erosions or other risk factors, since many patients don't have another one for years. This patient has had gout for 10 years, 3 or 4 flares a year, tophi on exam and a urate of 9.8. Tophi are a strong indication for urate-lowering therapy because they cause joint destruction and won't go away without bringing urate down. Repeated prednisone bursts also carry their own harm.

body.stem:
A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his family found him difficult to arouse. He was last seen normal at bedtime. He takes oxycodone for chronic back pain and recently doubled his dose because of worsening pain after a fall. He also takes lisinopril for hypertension. He has never smoked and has no known lung disease.
He is breathing shallowly at 8/min. Pupils are pinpoint. Lungs are clear. He is at sea level, breathing room air. There are no signs of head trauma.
data: Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C (97.9 °F) · BP 112/68 mm Hg · pulse rate 62/min · oxygen saturation 84% (ambient air)
Examination: responds only to painful stimuli · no focal deficits · clear lungs with equal breath sounds · normal heart sounds
Arterial blood gas (room air): pH 7.24 · PaCO2 70 mm Hg · PaO2 52 mm Hg
Chest radiograph: clear lungs · normal heart size
Labs: glucose 104 mg/dL · hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL
body.ask: Which of the following best explains his hypoxemia?

reasons.A: A–a gradient ≈10 mm Hg: normal for age
reasons.E: He's at sea level on room air

explain.explanation: The answer is A, alveolar hypoventilation. Calculate the A–a gradient. Alveolar oxygen is 0.21 times 713, about 150, minus 70 divided by 0.8, about 87. That gives an alveolar PO2 of about 62, and his arterial PO2 is 52, so the gradient is about 10. The expected normal for a 68-year-old is about 21, so his gradient is normal. A normal gradient with a high PaCO2 means hypoventilation, here from opioid toxicity, and the fix is naloxone and ventilatory support. Shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion problems all widen the gradient. And he's at sea level on room air, so it's not low inspired oxygen. Teaching point: high PaCO2 with a normal A–a gradient is hypoventilation.
explain.pearl: Normal A–a gradient hypoxemia = hypoventilation or low inspired O2. PAO2 = FiO2 × 713 − PaCO2/0.8; normal gradient ≈ age/4 + 4.
explain.references: West JB. Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials. 11th ed. 2020.

summaries.title: Hypoxemia: start with the A–a gradient

rows: Opioid overdose, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular weakness

details.A: Correct. Alveolar hypoventilation means too little fresh air reaches the alveoli, so CO2 rises and alveolar O2 falls in step. Run the alveolar gas equation: 0.21 × 713 is about 150, minus 70/0.8 (about 87), gives a PAO2 near 62. With a PaO2 of 52, the A–a gradient is about 10, below the age-expected value of about 21 (age/4 + 4). A high PaCO2 with a normal gradient means the lungs themselves are fine and the problem is drive. His pinpoint pupils, rate of 8 and recent doubled oxycodone dose point to opioid-induced central hypoventilation. Treat with naloxone and ventilatory support.
details.B: Not here. A right-to-left shunt sends blood past alveoli without any gas exchange, as in lobar consolidation, atelectasis, ARDS, an intracardiac defect or pulmonary AV malformations. Its signature is a wide A–a gradient and hypoxemia that barely improves with 100% oxygen, because the shunted blood never sees the added oxygen. This patient has clear lungs on exam and radiograph, and his A–a gradient is about 10, which is normal for age. His low PaO2 is fully explained by the high PaCO2 crowding oxygen out of the alveoli, so there's no shunt to find.
details.C: Not here. V/Q mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia, seen in COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia and interstitial disease. Some lung units get more blood than air, the gradient widens, and unlike shunt, supplemental oxygen corrects it well. The clue to V/Q mismatch is a PaO2 lower than the alveolar gas equation predicts. Here the predicted PAO2 is about 62 and the PaO2 is 52, a gradient of about 10, which is normal for a 68-year-old. He has no lung disease, a clear radiograph and an obvious reason to hypoventilate, so mismatch isn't the main driver.
details.D: Not here. Diffusion impairment comes from a thickened or reduced alveolar-capillary membrane, as in interstitial lung disease or emphysema. It typically shows up as exertional desaturation, because faster transit through the capillary leaves less time for oxygen to equilibrate, along with a reduced DLCO and a widened A–a gradient. At rest it's rarely the main cause of significant hypoxemia. This man has no known lung disease, clear lungs, a normal chest radiograph and a normal A–a gradient for age. The numbers point to low ventilation, not a membrane problem.
details.E: Not here. Low inspired oxygen is the other cause of hypoxemia with a normal A–a gradient. It happens at high altitude, where barometric pressure is lower, or when the inspired gas has a reduced oxygen fraction, such as in an enclosed space or a gas-delivery error. In that setting, PaCO2 is usually low, because hypoxemia drives hyperventilation. He is at sea level on room air, so FiO2 is 0.21 and barometric pressure is normal. His PaCO2 of 70 tells you the problem is not enough breathing, not thin air.

A 66-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis is seen urgently. She felt a pop behind her right knee while gardening yesterday, followed by calf pain and swelling. She walks her dog daily and is otherwise active. She has had no dyspnea, chest pain, or hemoptysis. She has had no recent surgery, travel, or immobilization, and no prior VTE. She takes acetaminophen as needed and no hormones.
The calf is tender and 3 cm larger than the left, with a crescent-shaped bruise below the medial malleolus.
data: Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C (98.2 °F) · BP 132/78 mm Hg · pulse rate 76/min · respiration rate 14/min · oxygen saturation 98% (ambient air)
Examination: crepitus of both knees · no knee effusion · clear lungs
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: Ultrasonography of the knee and calf

explain.explanation: The answer is B, ultrasonography of the knee and calf. A sudden pop behind the knee in someone with knee arthritis, followed by calf pain, swelling, and bruising tracking below the ankle, which is the crescent sign, suggests a ruptured Baker cyst. It mimics a DVT, so ultrasound is needed to tell them apart before anticoagulating. Empiric anticoagulation could cause bleeding into the calf. A D-dimer can be elevated in both. Teaching point: calf swelling after a knee pop, ultrasound for Baker cyst versus DVT.
explain.pearl: Ruptured Baker (popliteal) cyst mimics DVT: posterior knee 'pop', calf pain and swelling, crescent sign (bruising below the malleolus). Ultrasonography distinguishes cyst rupture from DVT. Treat the underlying knee arthritis.
explain.references: Herman AM, Marzo JM. Popliteal cysts: a current review. Orthopedics. 2014;37:e678.

details.A: Premature. Empiric anticoagulation is reasonable when DVT is highly likely and imaging will be delayed, provided bleeding risk is low. Here a sudden pop behind the knee in someone with knee arthritis, followed by calf swelling and a crescent-shaped bruise below the medial malleolus, points to a ruptured Baker cyst, and she has no VTE risk factors. Anticoagulating a cyst rupture can turn it into a calf hematoma or compartment syndrome. Ultrasound is quick, so get it first.
details.B: Correct. A pop behind the knee during activity in someone with knee osteoarthritis, followed by calf pain, 3 cm of calf swelling and bruising tracking below the medial malleolus (the crescent sign), is a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst. Joint fluid escapes through a posteromedial capsular connection into the calf. It mimics DVT and the two can coexist, so ultrasound of the knee and calf is the next step: it shows the cyst or fluid tracking down the calf and evaluates the deep veins with compression. Treat with rest, elevation, analgesia, and the underlying knee arthritis.
details.C: Doesn't distinguish. D-dimer is useful to exclude DVT or PE when pretest probability is low; a negative result makes VTE very unlikely. It's nonspecific and rises with hematoma, inflammation, older age and tissue injury, so a ruptured Baker cyst can raise it too. With a calf this swollen and tender, a positive result would still need ultrasound, and a negative one wouldn't explain her symptoms. Ultrasound answers both questions at once.
details.D: Not indicated. Knee arthroscopy is used for mechanical problems such as a locked knee from a displaced meniscal tear or loose bodies, and sometimes to wash out a septic joint. It has no benefit in degenerative knee OA and isn't needed to diagnose a ruptured Baker cyst. Rupture is managed conservatively, and treating the underlying arthritis, sometimes with an intra-articular steroid, reduces recurrence. It would add surgical and anesthesia risk without making the diagnosis that ultrasound can make in minutes.
details.E: No indication. CT pulmonary angiography is the test for suspected pulmonary embolism in someone with dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxemia, hemoptysis or tachycardia. She has none: respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98%, pulse 76 and clear lungs. It also exposes her to contrast and radiation and doesn't evaluate the calf. Her question is whether the calf swelling is a cyst or a clot, which ultrasound answers. If she later develops respiratory symptoms or DVT is found, the question of PE imaging can be revisited.

A 71-year-old man with 60 pack-years of smoking is seen in pulmonary clinic for severe exertional dyspnea that has worsened over 2 years. He now stops to rest after walking half a block. He has a mild dry cough and no wheezing, sputum, or chest pain. He quit smoking 3 years ago. He is a retired postal worker and has no bird or mold exposure. He uses tiotropium daily with little benefit.
He desaturates to 84% walking. CT shows upper-lobe emphysema and lower-lobe fibrosis. A lung specimen from the same condition is shown.
data: Vital signs: BP 132/80 mm Hg · pulse rate 88/min · respiration rate 18/min · oxygen saturation 93% at rest (ambient air)
Examination: BMI 24 · bibasilar fine crackles · digital clubbing · no wheezing
Spirometry and TLC: Near normal
DLCO: 28% predicted
body.ask: This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
body.image_credit: Yale Rosen from USA, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

reasons.C: CPFE carries high rates of PH and lung cancer

explain.explanation: The answer is C, pulmonary hypertension. This is combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema. The specimen shows emphysematous spaces next to honeycomb fibrosis. Physiologically, the hyperinflation of emphysema and the restriction of fibrosis cancel each other out, so spirometry and lung volumes can look almost normal, while the DLCO falls off a cliff and the patient desaturates with walking. CPFE carries a high rate of pulmonary hypertension, which drives prognosis, and a high rate of lung cancer. Teaching point: bad dyspnea, normal spirometry, terrible DLCO in a heavy smoker, think CPFE.
explain.pearl: Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema: severe dyspnea with near-normal spirometry and volumes (they cancel out) but a very low DLCO. Watch for pulmonary hypertension and lung cancer.
explain.references: Cottin V, et al. Syndrome of combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema: ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT research statement. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2022;206:e7.

details.A: Not the main risk. Spontaneous pneumothorax is a real complication of emphysema and other cystic lung disease: an older smoker with bullae suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, and the film shows a visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. CPFE patients can get pneumothoraces, but the word "only" makes this option wrong, and pneumothorax is not what drives his prognosis. His 84% exertional desaturation and DLCO of 28% point to severe gas-exchange and vascular loss, which is the setup for pulmonary hypertension, plus a high lung cancer risk.
details.B: Wrong disease. Hypercalcemia in lung disease comes from granulomas that make extra 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, as in sarcoidosis, TB, or fungal infection, or from PTHrP made by a squamous cell carcinoma. Sarcoid would give perilymphatic nodules and hilar adenopathy on CT, often in a younger patient with eye or skin findings. This man has upper-lobe emphysema plus lower-lobe fibrosis, which is combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema, not a granulomatous disease, so hypercalcemia is not his expected complication. Squamous cancer is a later possibility, but it isn't the answer to his current risk.
details.C: Correct. This is combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema: a heavy smoker with upper-lobe emphysema, lower-lobe fibrosis, basal crackles and clubbing. The emphysema raises compliance and the fibrosis lowers it, so spirometry and TLC look near normal while the DLCO collapses to 28% and he desaturates to 84% walking. Both processes destroy the capillary bed, and hypoxic vasoconstriction adds to it, so pulmonary hypertension is very common in CPFE and is the main driver of survival. Screen with an echocardiogram and confirm with right heart catheterization if it changes care. CPFE also carries a high rate of lung cancer, so keep imaging him.
details.D: Different disease. Bronchiectasis with Pseudomonas is the story of a patient with a daily productive cough, purulent sputum, and frequent exacerbations, often from cystic fibrosis, prior infection, or immune deficiency, with dilated, thick-walled airways on CT. Chronic Pseudomonas colonization marks worse disease and prompts eradication or inhaled antibiotics. This man has a mild dry cough with no sputum, and his CT shows emphysema and fibrosis rather than primary airway dilation. Traction bronchiectasis can appear inside fibrotic lung, but it isn't infected bronchiectasis and isn't his main risk.
details.E: No reversible obstruction. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is airway narrowing triggered by the cooling and drying of the airways during exercise. It shows up in asthmatics and athletes as cough, chest tightness and wheeze during or just after exertion, with an FEV1 drop of 10% or more after an exercise challenge, and it responds to albuterol before activity. This patient has no wheeze, his spirometry is near normal, and tiotropium hasn't helped. His exertional limit comes from gas exchange, with a DLCO of 28% and desaturation, not from bronchospasm.

A 48-year-old woman's husband noticed a mole on her upper back that has grown and changed color over 6 months. She cannot see the area herself and had not noticed it. It does not itch or bleed. She has fair skin and had several blistering sunburns as a child. She has never had skin cancer or a skin biopsy, and no one in her family has had melanoma.
She takes no medications and is otherwise healthy. It is 14 mm, asymmetric, with irregular borders and several shades of brown and black. A similar lesion is shown.
data: Vital signs: BP 118/74 mm Hg · pulse rate 70/min
Examination: about 30 small, uniform moles on the trunk and arms · no axillary, cervical or inguinal lymphadenopathy
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Superficial shave of the top only

body.image_credit: unknown author, Wikimedia Commons, public domain

reasons.D: Can transect it and miss depth

explain.explanation: The answer is E, an excisional biopsy with 1 to 3 millimeter margins. The lesion shows every melanoma warning sign: asymmetry, irregular borders, multiple colors, diameter over 6 mm, and evolution. An excisional biopsy removes the whole lesion with narrow margins so the pathologist can measure the Breslow thickness, which decides the definitive wide excision margins and whether sentinel node biopsy is needed. A superficial shave can cut through the tumor and make depth impossible to measure. Cryotherapy destroys it. Waiting is dangerous. Teaching point: suspected melanoma, narrow excisional biopsy first.
explain.pearl: Suspected melanoma (ABCDE: asymmetry, border, color, diameter, evolution): excisional biopsy with narrow 1–3 mm margins. Breslow thickness then decides wide-excision margins and sentinel node biopsy.
explain.references: Swetter SM, et al. AAD guidelines of care for primary cutaneous melanoma. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2019;80:208.

details.A: Destroys the evidence. Cryotherapy is used for benign lesions like seborrheic keratoses, warts and actinic keratoses, where tissue diagnosis isn't needed. Freezing a suspected melanoma destroys the tissue a pathologist needs to confirm the diagnosis and, more importantly, to measure Breslow thickness, which drives staging and treatment. It also doesn't reliably destroy the full depth of a melanoma, so tumor cells can remain and regrow under a scar. Her 14-mm asymmetric, multicolored, changing lesion needs a biopsy, not destruction.
details.B: Wrong order. Wide local excision is the definitive surgical treatment for melanoma, with margins set by Breslow thickness: 0.5 to 1 cm for melanoma in situ, 1 cm for tumors up to 1 mm, 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, and 2 cm for thicker tumors. You can't choose the right margin before the diagnosis and depth are known. A 2-cm excision upfront could be excessive for a thin melanoma, or a benign lesion, and wide excision before sentinel node mapping can disrupt lymphatic drainage. Biopsy comes first.
details.C: Dangerous delay. Rechecking in 3 to 6 months, often with photographs or dermoscopy, can be reasonable for a mildly atypical mole that hasn't changed. Her lesion has every ABCDE warning sign: asymmetry, irregular borders, several shades of brown and black, a diameter of 14 mm and evolution over 6 months noticed by her husband. Fair skin and blistering childhood sunburns add to her risk. Melanoma prognosis depends on thickness, which increases with time, so waiting 6 months could allow it to progress.
details.D: Risks missing depth. A superficial shave removes only the top layers of a lesion. It's acceptable for seborrheic keratoses or for diagnosing some superficial nonmelanoma skin cancers. For a suspected melanoma, a superficial shave can cut through the tumor, leaving the deeper portion behind. The pathologist then can't measure the true Breslow thickness, which determines staging, excision margins and whether sentinel node biopsy is needed. A deep saucerization shave that removes the whole lesion can be acceptable, but a 'top only' shave isn't.
details.E: Correct. A 14-mm mole on her back that is asymmetric, with irregular borders and several shades of brown and black, and that has grown and changed over 6 months, has all the ABCDE features of melanoma. Fair skin and blistering childhood sunburns add risk. An excisional biopsy with 1 to 3 mm margins removes the entire lesion down to the fat, so the pathologist can confirm melanoma and measure Breslow thickness, ulceration and mitotic rate. Those results decide the definitive wide excision margins and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed, which starts at a Breslow thickness of about 0.8 mm or with ulceration.

A 66-year-old woman comes for a routine visit. She feels well. She went through menopause at 51 and never took hormone therapy. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril. She has no history of fractures, takes no glucocorticoids, and has never had bone density testing. Her mother lived to 88 without a hip fracture.
She walks daily and doesn't smoke. She drinks one glass of wine a week and eats dairy most days. She has not lost height that she knows of.
data: Vital signs: BP 128/78 mm Hg · pulse rate 72/min · respiration rate 14/min
Examination: height 163 cm · weight 64 kg · BMI 24 · no kyphosis · no spinal tenderness · normal gait
Labs (last year): basic metabolic panel normal · TSH normal
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding osteoporosis?

choices.A: DXA of the hip and spine

explain.explanation: The answer is A, DXA of the hip and spine. Every woman 65 or older should have bone density screening, whether or not she has other risk factors. Younger postmenopausal women are screened when a risk tool like FRAX shows increased risk. Waiting for risk factors misses her age-based indication. Treatment comes after measurement. Heel ultrasound and spine radiographs aren't the standard. Teaching point: women 65 and older, get a DXA.
explain.pearl: USPSTF: screen with DXA all women ≥65, and postmenopausal women <65 at increased risk by a formal tool (e.g., FRAX). Evidence is insufficient for men. Don't repeat yearly after a normal result without new risk.
explain.references: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for osteoporosis to prevent fractures. JAMA. 2025.

details.A: Correct. The USPSTF recommends bone density screening for all women 65 and older, regardless of other risk factors. Postmenopausal women younger than 65 are screened if a formal tool such as FRAX shows increased risk. She is 66 and has never had a DXA, so she qualifies by age alone. Central DXA of the hip and lumbar spine is the standard: it gives the T-score used to diagnose osteoporosis (−2.5 or lower) or osteopenia (−1.0 to −2.5), and its femoral neck value feeds FRAX to estimate 10-year fracture risk. That result then guides whether to treat. After a normal result, repeating it every year without a new risk isn't needed.
details.B: Misses her indication. In postmenopausal women younger than 65, screening does depend on risk factors such as low body weight, smoking, glucocorticoid use, a parent with a hip fracture or heavy alcohol use, and a risk tool like FRAX guides the decision. But at 65 and older, age itself is the indication, because age is the strongest single predictor of fracture. She's 66, so the fact that she doesn't smoke, takes no steroids and has a mother without a hip fracture doesn't remove the need to screen her.
details.C: Measure first. Alendronate is a first-line oral bisphosphonate for osteoporosis, defined as a T-score of −2.5 or lower or a fragility fracture of the hip or spine, and for osteopenia when FRAX shows a 10-year hip fracture risk of 3 percent or more or a major osteoporotic fracture risk of 20 percent or more. She has no fracture and no bone density measurement, so there's no diagnosis to treat yet. Starting a drug empirically exposes her to esophageal irritation and rare long-term risks like atypical femur fracture without knowing she needs it.
details.D: Not the standard. Quantitative ultrasound of the heel is portable, cheap and radiation-free, and it's sometimes used at health fairs or in research. Low readings do predict fracture. But it measures a peripheral site, it doesn't give a T-score that can be used to diagnose osteoporosis by WHO criteria, it can't be used to follow response to treatment, and it doesn't match central DXA well. If a heel scan were done and abnormal, she'd still need a DXA. For a woman of 66, go straight to the test that diagnoses and guides treatment.
details.E: Not a screening test. Plain spine radiographs, or vertebral fracture assessment on DXA, are useful when you suspect a silent vertebral compression fracture, for example in someone with height loss of more than about 4 cm, new kyphosis or back pain, because a vertebral fracture by itself establishes osteoporosis and changes treatment. Radiographs can't measure bone density, and a bone has to lose a large share of its mineral before it looks thin on a film. She has no height loss, kyphosis or spinal tenderness, so radiographs add radiation without answering the question.

body.stem: A 58-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has 3 months of watery diarrhea, 6 to 8 times a day, including at night. The diarrhea is nonbloody and sometimes urgent, with mild cramping. She has lost 2 kg. She has not traveled or taken antibiotics, and no one at home is ill. She takes levothyroxine, sertraline, and naproxen most days; her levothyroxine dose has not changed, and her TSH is normal. Colonoscopy appears normal, and random colon biopsies show a thickened subepithelial collagen band. Stopping naproxen for 4 weeks did not help. Stool studies, including C. difficile testing and culture, are negative. She does not smoke.
data: Vital signs: BP 124/76 mm Hg · pulse rate 78/min · BMI 26
Examination: nontender abdomen · normal bowel sounds
Labs: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL · potassium 3.7 mEq/L · albumin 4.0 g/dL · IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase negative
body.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

reasons.E: Only if celiac disease is present

explain.explanation: The answer is D, oral budesonide. A middle-aged woman with chronic watery diarrhea, including at night, a normal-looking colon, and a thick collagen band on random biopsies has collagenous colitis, a type of microscopic colitis. Naproxen and sertraline are both associated triggers. Stopping the NSAID didn't help, so the next step is budesonide, which has the best evidence. Sertraline is worth reviewing too. Mesalamine doesn't work well here. There's no C. diff. Biologics are for rare refractory cases. And a gluten-free diet is only for coexisting celiac disease, which is associated and worth checking. Teaching point: watery diarrhea, normal scope, collagen band, budesonide.
explain.pearl: Microscopic colitis: chronic watery (often nocturnal) diarrhea in middle-aged women, normal-appearing colon, diagnosis only by biopsy. Stop culprit drugs (NSAIDs, SSRIs, PPIs); budesonide has the best evidence. No increased colon cancer risk.
explain.references: Nguyen GC, et al. AGA Institute guideline on the medical management of microscopic colitis. Gastroenterology. 2016;150:242.

summaries.title: Chronic diarrhea: clues to the cause

rows: Woman 45–60, nocturnal watery diarrhea, normal colonoscopy
SIBO → breath test or antibiotic trial

summaries.refs: Nguyen GC, et al. AGA Institute guideline on the medical management of microscopic colitis. Gastroenterology. 2016;150:242.

details.A: Doesn't work here. Mesalamine, a 5-ASA drug, is first-line therapy for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, where it acts topically on inflamed mucosa. In microscopic colitis, randomized trials found mesalamine no better than placebo and clearly inferior to budesonide, and guidelines recommend against it. She has collagenous colitis, a thick subepithelial collagen band on biopsy with normal-looking mucosa, and stopping naproxen didn't help. The drug with proven benefit for her is budesonide.
details.B: No infection to treat. Oral vancomycin is first-line therapy for C. difficile infection, along with fidaxomicin, and it is used when a patient has diarrhea with a positive toxin or PCR test, often after antibiotics. Her stool studies, including C. difficile testing, are negative, she hasn't had antibiotics, and her colonoscopy and biopsies show collagenous colitis, which is a noninfectious inflammatory condition. Treating her with vancomycin would add cost and microbiome disruption without addressing the cause.
details.C: Too soon. Infliximab and other biologics, such as adalimumab and vedolizumab, have been used in small series for microscopic colitis that doesn't respond to budesonide, depends on it, or relapses frequently. That is a small subset of patients, and the evidence is limited. Her diarrhea hasn't been treated with budesonide at all, so she isn't refractory. Starting with immunosuppression that requires TB and hepatitis B screening would skip the step that works for most patients.
details.D: Correct. A 58-year-old woman with 3 months of watery, nonbloody, nocturnal diarrhea, a normal-looking colonoscopy, and a thickened subepithelial collagen band on random biopsies has collagenous colitis, a form of microscopic colitis. Microscopic colitis is common in older women and is associated with autoimmune disease such as thyroid disease and celiac disease. It is also associated with drugs, especially NSAIDs, SSRIs, and PPIs. Stopping naproxen didn't help, and her sertraline is worth reviewing. Oral budesonide, typically 9 mg daily for about 8 weeks and then tapered, has the strongest evidence for inducing remission. Relapse after stopping is common.
details.E: Only for celiac disease. A gluten-free diet treats celiac disease, which is associated with microscopic colitis and can coexist with it. Celiac should be checked in patients with microscopic colitis, especially if they don't respond to budesonide. Her IgA tTG is negative, and her albumin is normal. Without celiac disease, a gluten-free diet wouldn't treat collagenous colitis. Her treatment should target the colonic inflammation shown on biopsy, starting with budesonide.
